title: Episode 19: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet
description: NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver commands for GitHub and VS Code.
concepts: NVDA essential navigation: headings, landmarks, forms, tables, links
NVDA browse mode versus focus mode
VoiceOver on macOS: rotor, VO keys, web navigation
GitHub keyboard shortcuts: ?, g i, g p, /, t, y, l
VS Code screen reader shortcuts: accessible help, accessible diff viewer
Quick navigation patterns for common tasks
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. This episode is a practical companion you can keep beside you while working on GitHub with a screen reader. It pairs especially well with the earlier lessons on understanding GitHub, navigating repositories, and the VS Code interface. And one administrative note up front: there is also a listen-first-or-review-later version of this appendix in the course podcast list, so learners can preview the concepts before reading or use the audio afterward to reinforce them.

[JAMIE]
So this is less of a theory episode and more of a working reference?

[ALEX]
Exactly. Think of it as an audio cheat sheet for GitHub navigation with NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver. The big promise is keyboard-only navigation, no mouse required. And the advice in the written companion is to keep the sheet open in a second window or print it, because the commands are organized by task.

[JAMIE]
And that matters for different kinds of learners, right? Not just screen reader users.

[ALEX]
Yes. For screen reader users, the sheet itself is designed to be navigated by heading, and the Elements List or Rotor can show all the sections at once. Tables are used heavily, with commands on the left and actions on the right. For low-vision learners, the recommendation is side-by-side reference, zooming to around one hundred fifty to two hundred percent, and noticing that key names are visually marked in code formatting. For sighted keyboard users, the guidance is to scan task-based sections, use the grouped command reference by screen reader, and bookmark the page as a fast reference.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Before we do anything on GitHub, we need the core mental model: two screen reader modes on the web.

[JAMIE]
This is the part that confuses people when a key suddenly does one thing on one page and something completely different in a text box.

[ALEX]
Exactly. First, Browse Mode, also called Virtual Cursor or Reading Mode. This is the mode for reading and moving through a web page. In this mode, the screen reader captures keys and turns them into navigation commands. So pressing H does not type the letter h. It jumps to the next heading.

[JAMIE]
How do learners know they are in that mode?

[ALEX]
With NVDA, there is a lower-pitched sound when switching, and NVDA may announce browse mode. With JAWS, you may hear virtual cursor on. VoiceOver on macOS works a bit differently. It does not use the same browse-versus-focus toggle language in the same way. Instead, you rely on VoiceOver commands and interaction.

[JAMIE]
And the other mode is for typing.

[ALEX]
Right. Focus Mode, sometimes called Forms Mode or Application Mode. This is where keystrokes go to the web page itself, not to the screen reader's web navigation system. You need it for text fields, comment boxes, issue titles, pull request descriptions, and interactive controls.

[JAMIE]
What are the toggles?

[ALEX]
For NVDA, NVDA plus Space, which is often Insert plus Space or Caps Lock plus Space depending on your setup. For JAWS, JAWS plus Z, usually Insert plus Z, though forms mode may also switch automatically. For VoiceOver, the common action is VO plus Shift plus Down Arrow to interact with an element, and VO plus Shift plus Up Arrow to stop interacting.

[JAMIE]
So the rule of thumb is simple.

[ALEX]
Browse mode to navigate. Focus mode to type.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let’s build your navigation toolkit. In Browse Mode, single-letter quick navigation is your best friend on GitHub. And for VoiceOver users, many of these same letters work when Quick Nav is enabled, while the Rotor remains a major navigation tool.

[JAMIE]
If someone memorizes only one category, which should it be?

[ALEX]
Headings. GitHub pages are structured with headings, and heading navigation is often the fastest way to move. H goes to the next heading. Shift plus H goes to the previous heading. Number keys let you jump by heading level: 1 for the next level-one heading, 2 for level two, 3 for level three, 4 for level four, and so on.

[JAMIE]
Why does that matter specifically on GitHub?

[ALEX]
Because page titles, section labels, issue titles, pull request titles, and commit headings are often marked with heading levels. The cheat sheet even calls out that issue and pull request titles are commonly level-three headings, and commit titles in pull requests can appear as level-four headings. So if you know the structure, you can move fast.

[JAMIE]
What about jumping across page regions instead of content items?

[ALEX]
That is landmark navigation. On NVDA and JAWS-style browse navigation, D goes to the next landmark, and Shift plus D goes to the previous one. JAWS also commonly uses R for the next region. VoiceOver users usually open the Rotor with VO plus U and choose Landmarks.

[JAMIE]
And GitHub uses landmarks a lot.

[ALEX]
It does. Common landmarks include the navigation menu with your avatar and global navigation, repository navigation with tabs like Code, Issues, Pull Requests, and Actions, the main landmark for primary content, repository files navigation near the README or files area, pull requests list, search results list, add a comment, and pagination.

[JAMIE]
That sounds incredibly useful when a page feels huge.

[ALEX]
It is. Landmarks let you skip broad regions before refining with headings or links.

[JAMIE]
What about links, buttons, and form fields?

[ALEX]
K moves to the next link in many browse systems, with Shift plus K for previous. B moves to the next button, Shift plus B for previous. F, and sometimes E depending on the reader, moves to the next form field or edit field. Tab and Shift plus Tab move among interactive elements in general. Enter or Space activates a control, and VoiceOver often uses VO plus Space to activate.

[JAMIE]
And lists and tables?

[ALEX]
Also important. L goes to the next list. I goes to the next list item. T goes to the next table. That matters a lot on GitHub because repository file listings are often table-like structures, and once you are in a table, control plus alt with arrow keys is the classic navigation pattern for moving between cells and rows.

[JAMIE]
So if I am trying to inspect files in a repository, T might get me there faster than tabbing forever.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now for one of the most powerful features in this whole appendix: the Elements List, or the Rotor in VoiceOver.

[JAMIE]
This is the tool people forget exists, and then once they learn it, everything changes.

[ALEX]
Very true. It opens a list of major page elements so you can jump directly where you need to go. In NVDA, use NVDA plus F7. In JAWS, Insert plus F6 opens the headings list, and Insert plus F7 opens the links list. In VoiceOver, VO plus U opens the Rotor, where you can switch among headings, links, landmarks, form controls, tables, and more.

[JAMIE]
Walk us through the actual workflow.

[ALEX]
Open the list or Rotor. Move between element categories, such as Headings, Links, Buttons, Form Controls, or Landmarks. Type to filter if your screen reader supports that list filtering. For example, type new issue to find a New Issue button or link quickly. Then press Enter, or the VoiceOver activation command, to jump there.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just a nice feature. It is a navigation superpower on complex pages.

[ALEX]
Exactly the phrase the appendix uses.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s make this concrete by reviewing the per-screen-reader command references.

[JAMIE]
Start with NVDA.

[ALEX]
On Windows with NVDA, browse-mode single-key navigation includes H and Shift plus H for next and previous heading, 1 through 6 for heading levels, K for link, B for button, F or E for form field, T for table, D for landmark, L for list, and I for list item.

[JAMIE]
And reading and mode control?

[ALEX]
Insert plus Space toggles Browse and Focus modes. Insert plus F7 opens the Elements List. NVDA plus Down Arrow starts reading from the cursor, often called Say All. NVDA plus Up Arrow reads the current line. Control stops reading.

[JAMIE]
Now JAWS.

[ALEX]
JAWS on Windows has very similar virtual-cursor navigation: H and Shift plus H for headings, 1 through 6 for heading levels, U for next unvisited link, K for next link, B for next button, F for next form field, T for next table, R for next landmark region, L for next list, and I for next list item.

[JAMIE]
And the mode and reading commands?

[ALEX]
Insert plus Z toggles the Virtual PC Cursor, which is the browse-versus-focus style control. Numpad Plus exits forms mode and reopens the PC cursor. Insert plus F6 is the headings list. Insert plus F7 is the links list. Insert plus Down Arrow starts reading from cursor. Insert plus Up Arrow reads the current line. Control stops reading.

[JAMIE]
And VoiceOver on macOS.

[ALEX]
First, VoiceOver itself starts or stops with Command plus F5. The VoiceOver modifier, abbreviated VO, is Control plus Option. VO plus U opens the Rotor. VO plus Right and VO plus Left move forward or backward. VO plus Space activates the current element. VO plus Shift plus Down Arrow interacts with an element, which is often how you effectively enter a focus-like mode. VO plus Shift plus Up Arrow stops interacting. VO plus A reads from the cursor. Control stops reading.

[JAMIE]
The appendix also gives study advice here, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Practice by page type. Don’t try to memorize everything at once. Move to the section matching the GitHub page you are on, read each table left to right as goal then key sequence, and rehearse one workflow at a time. For low-vision learners, the compact tables are meant to remain readable at high zoom, and the key sequences are visually distinguished.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
All right. Let’s get into actual GitHub pages. When someone lands on a repository main page, what should they expect?

[ALEX]
A repository page usually has a page title heading, repository navigation tabs such as Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, and sometimes Projects or Wiki, then a main content region with the file list and README. A very practical strategy is: first jump to the main landmark, then use heading navigation to orient, then jump to the repository navigation landmark if you need tabs, and use table navigation or links to move through the file list.

[JAMIE]
And if the file list is hard to find?

[ALEX]
Try T for the next table, or use the Elements List or Rotor to find relevant headings and landmarks. Also, tabbing can work, but it is usually slower than jumping by structure.

[JAMIE]
What about the issues list page?

[ALEX]
On an issues list, listen for the main region and page heading, then find the search results list or issues list area. Use headings to jump between sections, lists to identify the results area, and links to move among issue titles. If you need the New Issue control, the Elements List or Rotor is often the fastest way to locate it by name.

[JAMIE]
And once you open a single issue?

[ALEX]
On the issue detail page, the issue title is a major anchor point. From there, you may navigate to metadata, the description, timeline items, comments, and eventually the Add a comment form. Headings help you move among major sections. Landmarks can jump you to the main content or comment area. And when you reach the comment box or another edit field, you switch into Focus Mode or interact mode before typing.

[JAMIE]
Pull request lists are similar to issue lists?

[ALEX]
Very similar. You are generally moving through lists of pull request titles and status information. Again, headings, landmarks, and links are the fastest route, and the search results list or pull requests list landmark can be a strong anchor.

[JAMIE]
Then on a pull request detail page, things branch out into tabs.

[ALEX]
Yes. The pull request detail page usually includes tabs such as Conversation, Commits, and Files Changed. The Conversation tab behaves a lot like an issue timeline, with the title, description, review activity, and comments. Headings and landmarks are your map. The Add a comment landmark or form field is especially important when you want to review or respond.

[JAMIE]
What changes on the Commits tab?

[ALEX]
The Commits tab often contains a list of commit entries, each of which may be exposed with heading-like structure or linked text. Heading-level navigation, lists, and links all help. The appendix specifically reminds learners that level-four headings may correspond to commit titles in pull requests, which can help if your reader supports heading-level jumps cleanly.

[JAMIE]
And the Files Changed tab is often the hardest one.

[ALEX]
Yes, because diffs and code views can be dense. Use headings and landmarks first to find the file or diff region, then use tables or structured navigation where available. This is also a place where GitHub feature previews or accessibility improvements may change the experience, so the appendix includes a specific note about checking and enabling feature previews.

[JAMIE]
How does that work?

[ALEX]
The core idea is that GitHub sometimes rolls out interface changes behind previews or feature flags. If the page does not match the instructions, check whether a preview is enabled or whether the interface has changed. For NVDA and JAWS users, browse mode navigation helps inspect settings pages and dialogs. For VoiceOver users, the Rotor and interaction commands are the main tools for reaching and changing those settings.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s talk about typing, because this is where many learners get tripped up.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. To enter text on GitHub, Focus Mode or interaction is required. On NVDA, that often means toggling with NVDA plus Space if it did not switch automatically. On JAWS, Insert plus Z or automatic forms mode may handle it. On VoiceOver, interact with the text area using VO plus Shift plus Down Arrow.

[JAMIE]
And how do you know it worked?

[ALEX]
The most practical test is simple: type a letter. If the screen reader tries to use it as a navigation key, you are still in Browse Mode. If the letter goes into the field, you are in the right mode.

[JAMIE]
The appendix also mentions markdown shortcuts inside GitHub text areas.

[ALEX]
Yes. While the exact set can vary by platform and editor behavior, the important teaching point is that GitHub text areas support common markdown formatting workflows. So when you are in Focus Mode, you can use familiar keyboard shortcuts to format text efficiently. The key accessibility point is that those shortcuts only help once you are truly inside the editable field.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now, dropdown menus and flyouts.

[JAMIE]
These can be awkward because they look simple visually, but keyboard focus can jump around.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The general strategy is to move to the button that opens the menu, activate it, then navigate within the flyout using Tab, Shift plus Tab, arrow keys where supported, or screen-reader structural commands if the menu is exposed semantically. For VoiceOver users in particular, interacting with the menu or popover content may be necessary before its controls become easy to traverse.

[JAMIE]
So VoiceOver users should be ready to use interact and stop interacting as part of the workflow.

[ALEX]
Yes. That is explicitly called out.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s move into GitHub’s own built-in keyboard shortcuts. These are separate from the screen reader’s commands.

[ALEX]
Right, and that distinction matters. Screen reader commands move you through accessibility structure. GitHub shortcuts trigger GitHub actions. The art is using them together without conflict.

[JAMIE]
What is the overall advice?

[ALEX]
Use GitHub shortcuts alongside a screen reader thoughtfully. Make sure you are not in a text field unless the shortcut is intended for text editing. Be aware of Browse Mode intercepting letters. And when GitHub uses G-based shortcut sequences, there is a practical sequence to follow.

[JAMIE]
What does that mean?

[ALEX]
GitHub has multi-key shortcuts like pressing G and then another key to go somewhere. If your screen reader is in a mode where single letters are navigation commands, the initial G may never reach GitHub. So the practical sequence is: ensure you are in the right mode, often focus-like interaction on the page body or a state where GitHub can receive the keys, then press the GitHub shortcut sequence.

[JAMIE]
And if you forget what shortcuts are available?

[ALEX]
Press question mark on GitHub to open the shortcut dialog. That is a built-in discoverability feature. Then read the dialog with your screen reader like any other modal: use headings, read line by line, tab through controls, or use the Rotor or Elements List as appropriate.

[JAMIE]
The appendix breaks these shortcuts down by page type too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Site-wide shortcuts work on every GitHub page. Repository navigation shortcuts work on any repository page. There are also groups for source code browsing while viewing a file, issue and pull request lists, issue and pull request detail pages, comments while inside any text area with Focus Mode required, the Files Changed tab in pull requests, the Notifications page, GitHub Actions, and Projects in board and table view.

[JAMIE]
So the teaching goal is not to memorize every GitHub shortcut from audio.

[ALEX]
Correct. The goal is to know that these categories exist, know that question mark reveals them, and know how to let GitHub receive the keys instead of your screen reader intercepting them.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The appendix also provides quick-reference navigation patterns. These are habits you can repeat across pages.

[JAMIE]
Such as?

[ALEX]
A simple pattern is: jump to main, scan headings, use landmarks to change regions, open the Elements List or Rotor if you feel lost, move to the target form field, switch to Focus Mode to type, then return to Browse Mode to keep navigating. Another pattern is to use headings for orientation, links for selection, and tables for structured content like file lists.

[JAMIE]
That kind of pattern is reassuring because it scales across a lot of GitHub.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You do not need a different mental model for every page.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now troubleshooting. This may be the most emotionally important part, because when things do not match the lesson, learners often assume they did something wrong.

[ALEX]
Yes, and often they did not. First issue: the page does not match the instructions. That can happen because GitHub’s interface changes, experiments are rolled out gradually, or feature previews alter the layout. The advice is to reorient using headings and landmarks rather than expecting every control in exactly the same place, and to check feature preview settings if relevant.

[JAMIE]
Second problem: I’m hearing too much or navigating too slowly.

[ALEX]
That usually means you are reading linearly when structural navigation would be faster. Use H for headings, D or the Rotor for landmarks, T for tables, and especially the Elements List or Rotor to jump directly. Also remember the read-all and stop-reading commands so you can control pace.

[JAMIE]
Third: I pressed H but it’s typing the letter h.

[ALEX]
That is the classic mode mismatch. You are probably in Focus Mode or inside an editable field. Exit forms or interaction mode if your goal is navigation. On NVDA, toggle with NVDA plus Space. On JAWS, use Insert plus Z or leave forms mode, often with Numpad Plus. On VoiceOver, stop interacting with VO plus Shift plus Up Arrow if needed.

[JAMIE]
Fourth: I can’t find the comment box.

[ALEX]
Use landmarks like Add a comment, jump by form fields with F, search the Elements List or Rotor for comment-related controls, and remember the box may be below a long timeline. Once you reach it, switch into Focus Mode before typing.

[JAMIE]
And the code or diff area is hard to navigate.

[ALEX]
That is common. Start broader. Find the file or diff heading first, then move within the region using tables, links, or line-by-line reading as appropriate. If the layout seems unfamiliar, check whether a feature preview or interface change is affecting the page. And give yourself permission to use multiple strategies, not just one key.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Near the end, the appendix points learners to official screen reader resources.

[JAMIE]
Why include that in a course appendix?

[ALEX]
Because this sheet is practical, but it does not replace the official documentation for your screen reader or the platform standards behind accessible web behavior. Learners are encouraged to consult GitHub Docs, especially keyboard shortcut documentation, GitHub’s changelog for interface updates, the W3C WCAG overview, WAI tutorials for accessible design patterns, and the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide.

[JAMIE]
So if something behaves differently, those are part of your evidence trail.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The appendix also reminds learners that related keyboard shortcuts appear in other appendices, so this is one reference among several in the course.

[JAMIE]
And there is a compatibility note too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Screen reader compatibility is never perfectly frozen. If a command does not work as described, possibilities include a different key map, laptop keyboard differences, Quick Nav being off, VoiceOver interaction state, a GitHub UI change, browser differences, or screen reader version changes. The key idea is not that you failed. It is that accessibility workflows are version-sensitive, and authoritative sources should be checked when behavior differs.

[JAMIE]
And the appendix closes with an authoritative-source map.

[ALEX]
Right. It ties sections back to dependable references such as GitHub Docs, the GitHub changelog, WCAG overview pages, WAI tutorials, and WAI-ARIA practices. That is a reminder that this cheat sheet is grounded in broader accessibility guidance, not isolated tips.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
If you had to leave learners with a compact practice routine after this episode, what would it be?

[ALEX]
Open a GitHub page. Jump to main. Use H to sample headings. Use D, R, or the Rotor to inspect landmarks. Open the Elements List or Rotor and practice jumping to a known target like New Issue or Add a comment. Enter Focus Mode only when it is time to type. Exit when it is time to navigate. And if GitHub’s own shortcuts are needed, make sure GitHub, not the screen reader, receives the keystrokes.

[JAMIE]
And emotionally?

[ALEX]
Do not judge yourself by speed on the first pass. This is pattern learning. Once headings, landmarks, lists, tables, elements lists, and mode switching become automatic, GitHub becomes much more predictable.

[JAMIE]
That is a great note to end on.

[ALEX]
Thanks for learning with us. Keep this cheat sheet nearby, practice on one page type at a time, and come back to it whenever a workflow feels rusty.

# Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet
>
> **Listen to Episode 19:** [Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 02: Understanding GitHub](02-understanding-github.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 03](03-navigating-repositories.md), [Chapter 11](11-vscode-interface.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: Keyboard shortcuts](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/accessibility/keyboard-shortcuts)

## GitHub Navigation with NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver

> **How to use this sheet:** Keep it open in a second window or print it. Commands are organized by task so you can find what you need quickly while you work. All commands are keyboard-only - no mouse required.

### Learning Cards: Using This Cheat Sheet

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Use heading navigation (H key) to jump between task categories -- each section is an h2 heading
- Open the Elements List (NVDA+F7 or Insert+F6) and switch to the Headings tab to see all sections at once
- Tables list commands in the left column and actions in the right -- use Ctrl+Alt+Arrow keys to navigate

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Keep this open in a second browser tab or print it for side-by-side reference while working
- Command tables are compact -- increase zoom to 150-200% and the two-column layout stays readable
- Key names are in backtick code formatting which gives them a distinct visual border

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Sections are organized by task (navigation, typing, dropdowns, troubleshooting) -- scan the h2 headings
- The "Per-Screen-Reader Command Reference" section groups everything by NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver
- Bookmark this page -- it is the single fastest reference when you forget a key combination

</details>

## Screen Reader Mode Basics

Before navigating GitHub, understand the two fundamental modes that all screen readers use on the web:

### Browse Mode (also called Virtual Cursor / Reading Mode)

This is your primary mode for **reading and navigating** pages. The screen reader intercepts keystrokes and uses them as navigation commands - for example, pressing `H` jumps to the next heading rather than typing the letter H.

| Screen Reader | How to know you're in Browse Mode |
| ---------------  | ----------------------------------  |
| **NVDA** | Lower-pitched sound when switching; NVDA says "browse mode" |
| **JAWS** | JAWS says "virtual cursor on" |
| **VoiceOver** | No mode switching needed - VoiceOver uses the VO modifier keys |

### Focus Mode (also called Forms or Application Mode)

This mode is for **typing and interacting** with form fields, text areas, buttons, and interactive widgets. Your keystrokes go directly to the web page instead of being captured by the screen reader.

| Screen Reader | Toggle Focus/Browse Mode | When to use |
| ---------------  | --------------------------  | -------------  |
| **NVDA** | `NVDA+Space` (Insert+Space or CapsLock+Space) | Type in comment boxes, issue titles, PR descriptions |
| **JAWS** | `JAWS+Z` (Insert+Z) or automatic | Same |
| **VoiceOver** | `VO+Shift+Down` to interact with an element | Same |

> **Rule of thumb:** Browse mode to navigate, Focus mode to type.

## Quick Navigation Keys (Browse Mode)

These single-key shortcuts work in Browse Mode (NVDA and JAWS). VoiceOver users with Quick Nav enabled use the same keys.

### Heading Navigation - Your Most-Used Tool

GitHub structures pages with headings. Jumping between headings is the fastest way to navigate.

| Key | Action | VoiceOver |
| -----  | --------  | -----------  |
| `H` | Next heading (any level) | `H` (Quick Nav on) |
| `Shift+H` | Previous heading | `Shift+H` |
| `1` | Next h1 (page title) | `1` |
| `2` | Next h2 (section heading) | `2` |
| `3` | Next h3 (issue/PR titles are h3) | `3` |
| `4` | Next h4 (commit titles in PRs) | `4` |

### Landmark Navigation - Jump Between Page Regions

Landmarks are named regions of a page (navigation, main content, sidebar, etc.). GitHub uses landmarks heavily.

| Key | Action | VoiceOver |
| -----  | --------  | -----------  |
| `D` | Next landmark / region | `VO+U` → Landmarks rotor |
| `Shift+D` | Previous landmark | Same, navigate backwards |

#### GitHub landmarks you will encounter

| Landmark Label | What It Contains |
| ----------------  | -----------------  |
| Navigation Menu | Your avatar menu and global nav |
| Repository navigation | Code, Issues, PRs, Actions tabs |
| Main | The primary page content |
| Repository files navigation | README display |
| Pull requests list | The list of PRs |
| Search Results List | Issues or PR list results |
| Add a comment | Comment submission form |
| Pagination | Next/Previous page buttons |

### Link, Button, and Form Navigation

| Key | Action | JAWS Equivalent | VoiceOver |
| -----  | --------  | -----------------  | -----------  |
| `K` | Next link | `Tab` or `U` | `VO+U` → Links rotor |
| `Shift+K` | Previous link | `Shift+U` | - |
| `B` | Next button | `B` | `VO+U` → Buttons rotor |
| `Shift+B` | Previous button | `Shift+B` | - |
| `F` or `E` | Next edit/form field | `F` | `VO+U` → Form Controls |
| `Tab` | Next interactive element (any type) | `Tab` | `Tab` |
| `Shift+Tab` | Previous interactive element | `Shift+Tab` | `Shift+Tab` |
| `Enter` / `Space` | Activate link or button | Same | `VO+Space` |

### List and Table Navigation

| Key | Action | Notes |
| -----  | --------  | -------  |
| `L` | Next list | Useful for spotting issue/PR lists |
| `I` | Next list item | Navigate within a list |
| `T` | Next table | **Use this for the files table in a repo** |
| `Ctrl+Alt+→` | Move right in a table cell | Navigate table columns |
| `Ctrl+Alt+←` | Move left in a table cell | |
| `Ctrl+Alt+↓` | Move down in a table (next row) | Navigate file list rows |
| `Ctrl+Alt+↑` | Move up in a table | |

## The Elements List - Your Navigation Superpower

This is one of the most powerful tools for navigating complex pages. It opens a dialog listing all headings, links, buttons, form fields, or landmarks on the page.

| Screen Reader | Open Elements List | What It Shows |
| ---------------  | -------------------  | ---------------  |
| **NVDA** | `NVDA+F7` (Insert+F7 or CapsLock+F7) | Headings, Links, Form fields, Buttons, Landmarks (tabs within the dialog) |
| **JAWS** | `Insert+F6` (headings) / `Insert+F7` (links) | Headings list / Links list |
| **VoiceOver** | `VO+U` | Rotor - switch between Headings, Links, Landmarks, Form Controls |

### How to use it

1. Press the keyboard shortcut above
2. Navigate between the tabs (Headings, Links, etc.) with `Tab` or arrow keys
3. Type to filter the list (e.g., type "new issue" to find the New Issue button)
4. Press `Enter` to jump to the item on the page

### Checking and Enabling Feature Previews

GitHub Feature Previews are opt-in UI improvements. For screen reader users, two are especially important: **New Issues Experience** and **New Files Changed Experience**. Both may already be active - or may have graduated out of Feature Preview entirely.

#### NVDA / JAWS (Browse Mode)

| Goal | Key Sequence |
| ------  | --------------  |
| Open User Menu | `B` repeatedly until "Open user navigation menu, button" → `Enter` |

## Dropdown Menus and Flyouts

GitHub uses popup flyout menus for labels, assignees, reviewers, and branch selection. Here is how to handle them:

```text
Step 1: Navigate to the button (D for landmark, B for button, or Tab)
Step 2: Activate the button (Enter or Space) - flyout opens
Step 3: Type to filter results OR use ↑/↓ arrow keys to navigate
Step 4: Select an item (Enter)
Step 5: Close the flyout (Esc) - selections apply on close
```

### VoiceOver users

```text
Step 1: Navigate to the button with Tab or VO+Right
Step 2: Activate with VO+Space
Step 3: VO+Down to enter the flyout
Step 4: VO+Right/Left to navigate items
Step 5: VO+Space to select, Esc to close
```

## GitHub Built-In Keyboard Shortcuts

GitHub has a dedicated keyboard shortcut system built into every page. These are completely separate from your screen reader's navigation keys - they are JavaScript-powered shortcuts that trigger GitHub actions directly without using the mouse.

### Using GitHub shortcuts alongside a screen reader

The key issue: when your screen reader is in Browse Mode, it intercepts keystrokes before they reach the page. GitHub's shortcut system relies on the page receiving the keystroke directly. Here is how to unlock them:

| Screen Reader | How to use GitHub shortcuts |
| ---  | ---  |
| **NVDA** | Press `NVDA+Space` to enter Focus Mode, use the shortcut, then `NVDA+Space` to return to Browse Mode |
| **JAWS** | Press `Insert+Z` to toggle Virtual Cursor off, use the shortcut, then `Insert+Z` to turn it back on |
| **VoiceOver** | GitHub shortcuts generally work without mode switching - VoiceOver handles this differently |

**Exceptions that always work in Browse Mode:** `?` (shows all shortcuts) and `S`/`/` (focus the search bar) work at any time because they immediately move browser focus to an interactive element.

#### Practical sequence for `G` shortcuts

```text
Step 1: Press NVDA+Space (or Insert+Z in JAWS) - enter Focus Mode
Step 2: Press G, pause half a second
Step 3: Press the second key (I, P, A, etc.)
Step 4: Press NVDA+Space to return to Browse Mode on the new page
```

### Discover shortcuts on any page - The `?` Key

> **Start here every time you're on an unfamiliar GitHub page.** The `?` key opens GitHub's built-in keyboard shortcut help dialog. It lists every shortcut for the exact page you are on - the set changes depending on whether you are on a repository, an issue, a PR, the notifications inbox, etc.

Press `?` (Shift+/) from any GitHub page **when not inside a text field** to open the shortcut dialog.

#### Reading the shortcut dialog with a screen reader

The dialog is a standard ARIA modal (`role="dialog"`). When it opens, browser focus moves inside it automatically.

##### NVDA

```text
Step 1: Press Shift+/ to open the dialog → NVDA announces "dialog" and reads the title
Step 2: Press NVDA+Space to enter Browse Mode inside the dialog
Step 3: Press H to navigate between shortcut categories (they are h2 headings)
Step 4: Press ↓ to read each shortcut row in the category
Step 5: Press Escape or Tab to the Close button → Enter to close
```

##### JAWS

```text
Step 1: Press Shift+/ → JAWS announces the dialog and its title
Step 2: Use ↓ to read through the contents, or Ctrl+Home to start from the top
Step 3: Use Tab to move between interactive elements (the Close button)
Step 4: Press Escape to close
```

##### VoiceOver (macOS)

```text
Step 1: Press Shift+/ → VoiceOver announces the dialog
Step 2: Use VO+Right to move through the dialog contents
Step 3: Use VO+Command+H to jump between heading categories
Step 4: Press Escape or navigate to the Close button (VO+Space)
```

##### Key facts about the shortcut dialog

- It is **context-aware** - the shortcuts shown change based on your current page
- It is **always current** - GitHub automatically updates it when they add new shortcuts
- The dialog is divided into sections: Site-wide, Source code browsing, Issues, Pull requests, Notifications, etc. - only sections relevant to the current page appear
- You do not need to be in Focus Mode to open it - `?` works from Browse Mode

| `S` or `/` | Focus the search bar |
| `G` then `N` | Go to your Notifications |

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

### "The page doesn't match the instructions"

- **Solution:** Maximize your browser window. GitHub's layout changes at smaller widths, and landmarks/headings may appear in different positions. Full-screen or maximized window gives the most consistent experience.

### "I'm hearing too much or navigating too slowly"

- Disable hovercards in GitHub Accessibility Settings (see [Pre-Workshop Setup](00-pre-workshop-setup.md))
- Adjust your screen reader verbosity settings
- Use `NVDA+F7` / `VO+U` to get a filtered list rather than tabbing through everything
- **NVDA reads GitHub too slowly:** In NVDA Settings → Browse Mode → increase "Maximum number of characters on one line" to 10000. This prevents NVDA from pausing to wrap long lines.

### "I pressed H but it's typing the letter H"

- You are in **Focus Mode** - press `NVDA+Space` (or `JAWS+Z`) to return to Browse Mode
- In Browse Mode, H is a navigation key, not a typing key

### "I can't find the comment box"

- Use `D` to navigate to the "Add a comment" landmark
- Then `E` or `F` to jump to the edit field
- Switch to Focus Mode before typing

### "The diff/code area is hard to navigate"

- The Files Changed tab requires Focus Mode to navigate the diff table
- Use `NVDA+Space` to enter Focus Mode, then use arrow keys
- Use `Ctrl+Alt+Arrow` keys to move between table cells

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.
voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
